definition: situated at the back; later in time
memoryTip: Post = after/behind — rear end of the body, or what comes later.
correctPassage: In the diagram, the posterior section of the brain is shaded in blue.
wrongPassages: She booked a posterior appointment for first thing Monday morning.
The poster hung posterior on the bulletin board so everyone would see it first.
Investors chased a posterior market that had not moved a cent all year.

definition: a formal written request; to make such a request
memoryTip: A formal “please” on paper — you petition for action, not for fun.
correctPassage: Residents signed a petition asking the city to restore weekend bus service.
wrongPassages: She stuck a gold petition star on the chart to mark her highest score.
Bakers wrote “petition = 120 g flour” on the test-kitchen wall.
The coach called a petition timeout when the game got out of hand.

definition: required by law or rules; compulsory
memoryTip: Mandate = command — if it’s mandatory, skipping it isn’t allowed.
correctPassage: Safety training is mandatory for everyone who enters the laboratory.
wrongPassages: Attendance was mandatory only if you felt like showing up that day.
Critics called the ending mandatory because it answered every plot question early.
She kept a mandatory schedule of hobbies she could drop anytime.

definition: allowed; permitted under the rules
memoryTip: You have permission — permissible means it’s okay to do.
correctPassage: Under the new rules, only certain additives are permissible in the product.
wrongPassages: Speeding through the school zone is permissible if you’re running late.
She kept a permissible lock on the door that no one was allowed to open.
The judge ruled the evidence permissible because it had been illegally obtained.

definition: dependent on something else; a group representing a larger body
memoryTip: Tied to a contingency — it happens only if X happens first.
correctPassage: Approval is contingent on the environmental review being completed on time.
wrongPassages: Her mood was contingent: always the same no matter what happened.
They labeled the sealed vault contingent so nothing inside could ever change.
The permanent bridge was contingent on weather that never varies.

definition: use up or greatly reduce the supply of
memoryTip: De-plete (empty the plate) — drain the stock until little is left.
correctPassage: Overfishing continues to deplete stocks that once seemed inexhaustible.
wrongPassages: Rain helped deplete the reservoir until it overflowed its banks.
They hoped to deplete the food banks by donating truckloads of supplies.
A long rest will deplete your energy before the big race.

definition: comply with rules, standards, or prevailing norms
memoryTip: Con-form: take the same form as the rules or the group.
correctPassage: The design must conform to accessibility standards before construction begins.
wrongPassages: She refused to conform by carefully following every item in the dress code.
The rebel plan was to conform and break every rule on the first day.
Engineers made the bridge conform by ignoring the building code entirely.

definition: basic; involving only the simplest principles
memoryTip: Rude / raw basics — only the first, simplest steps, not advanced.
correctPassage: Even a rudimentary grasp of statistics helps readers evaluate the claims.
wrongPassages: Her rudimentary thesis won the award for the most sophisticated research of the year.
The surgeon described the twelve-hour procedure as rudimentary and routine.
They called the PhD-level textbook rudimentary because beginners could not open it.

definition: scarcity; smallness of number or amount
memoryTip: Pauc- = few (Latin) — a paucity means not many, almost none.
correctPassage: A paucity of reliable data made firm conclusions difficult.
wrongPassages: Shoppers complained about the paucity of choices in a store with thousands of brands.
The library’s paucity of books filled every shelf from floor to ceiling.
A paucity of rainfall flooded the valley for the third week in a row.

definition: the appearance of being true or real
memoryTip: Veri (truth) + similar — looks true-to-life, even if it’s fiction.
correctPassage: The novel’s careful period detail gives it a strong sense of verisimilitude.
wrongPassages: Her verisimilitude briefing covered risks, costs, and a recommendation in four slides.
The cartoon’s wild talking animals were praised for strict historical verisimilitude.
He demanded verisimilitude by inventing facts no one could check.

definition: find out for certain; determine
memoryTip: As-certain: make it certain — dig until you know for sure.
correctPassage: Investigators sought to ascertain whether the signal was natural or artificial.
wrongPassages: They hoped to ascertain confusion by adding three more optional steps to the form.
She tried to ascertain the answer by guessing without looking at any evidence.
Managers planned to ascertain the problem by refusing to investigate further.

definition: provide evidence to support a claim
memoryTip: Give the claim substance — back it up with proof, not vibes.
correctPassage: Without field measurements, the team could not substantiate its claim.
wrongPassages: He tried to substantiate the charge by shredding every document that mentioned it.
She hoped to substantiate the rumor by repeating it louder with no sources.
They moved to substantiate the theory by ignoring all conflicting data.

definition: remarkably great in size, amount, or degree
memoryTip: Prodigy-level scale — so large or impressive it stands out.
correctPassage: The archive preserves a prodigious number of letters from the period.
wrongPassages: He showed prodigious talent by barely finishing the simplest practice drill.
The gallery’s prodigious hang placed one tiny sketch on an otherwise empty wall.
Voters rejected the plan as prodigious because it cost almost nothing and changed little.

definition: involving deceit; obtained or done by deception
memoryTip: Fraud — dishonest, fake, or won by tricking someone.
correctPassage: Auditors uncovered fraudulent invoices submitted by a subcontractor.
wrongPassages: Judges called the thoroughly sourced opinion fraudulent after it cited every relevant case.
Her fraudulent tax return listed every income source exactly as required by law.
The charity’s fraudulent books balanced because every donation was honestly recorded.

definition: able to be touched or felt; so intense as to seem tangible
memoryTip: You can almost palm it — so clear or strong you can feel it.
correctPassage: Tension in the room was palpable as the results were announced.
wrongPassages: The difference between the two proposals was so palpable that no one could detect it.
Excitement was palpable in the empty hall where nobody showed up.
Admin tried to palpable complaints by hiding the public contact form.

definition: cause surprise or confusion; mix up or thwart
memoryTip: Con-found: throw into confusion — mix up or leave people stunned.
correctPassage: The unexpected results confound earlier models of the disease’s spread.
wrongPassages: Clear labels were added to confound shoppers who had been confused before.
She hoped to confound the mystery by publishing every clue in plain order.
Teachers used the answer key to confound students who already knew the material.

definition: pay no attention to; ignore
memoryTip: Dis + regard — drop your regard; treat it as if it doesn’t matter.
correctPassage: Critics accused the agency of disregard for community concerns.
wrongPassages: She showed complete disregard by reading every comment and answering each one.
The pilot’s disregard for the checklist meant he reviewed every step twice.
They planned to disregard the warning by posting it on every door in the building.

definition: emphasize or draw attention to
memoryTip: Like underlining a line — you underscore what matters most.
correctPassage: The new findings underscore the need for longer-term studies.
wrongPassages: He tried to underscore the point by mumbling it once and changing the subject.
Editors underscored the headline by deleting it from the front page entirely.
The report underscored safety risks by burying them in an unread appendix.

definition: conforming to traditional or established doctrine
memoryTip: Ortho = straight — by-the-book, traditional belief or method.
correctPassage: Her approach departed from orthodox methods used in the field for decades.
wrongPassages: His orthodox plan threw out every tradition the profession still followed.
Critics called the radical redesign orthodox for breaking every design rule.
She took an orthodox path by inventing a method no textbook had ever taught.

definition: the highest point; peak of power or success
memoryTip: Highest point in the sky — and the peak of a career or empire.
correctPassage: The empire reached its zenith under the rule of the second emperor.
wrongPassages: The company hit its zenith the year sales collapsed and half the staff left.
At the zenith of the valley, water collected in the lowest ditch.
Her career’s zenith was the unpaid internship she took right after college.
